lessons.title: Majors, Crosses and Exotic Pairs: Where the Rupee Fits

children.text: Open the currency derivatives segment on NSE and you will find USD/INR, EUR/INR, GBP/INR and JPY/INR. Scroll further and you will also see EUR/USD, GBP/USD and USD/JPY, pairs with no rupee in them at all. Meanwhile, a Telegram "forex guru" is posting calls on GBP/JPY and USD/TRY. These pairs behave very differently. Some trade trillions of dollars a day with spreads thinner than a hair. Others can lose a third of their value in a year. This lesson sorts every pair into its family and shows you exactly where the rupee sits.

body.text: Currencies form a pecking order with the US dollar at the centre. The more a pair trades, the cheaper, smoother and more predictable it is. The rupee is a large emerging-market currency, bigger than most of its peers but still well outside the top tier.

children.text: The Three Families of Currency Pairs

markDefs.definition: A pair made of the US dollar and one of the most traded developed-market currencies: EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, CAD, AUD or NZD.
In global markets, a pair of two major currencies that does not include the US dollar, such as EUR/GBP or EUR/JPY.
A pair of the US dollar, or another major, with a less traded or emerging-market currency, such as USD/TRY, USD/ZAR or USD/INR.

children.text: Dealers group pairs into three families.
Majors
pair the dollar with another heavyweight developed-market currency.
Crosses
pair two majors without the dollar.
Exotics
pair a major with an emerging or smaller currency. The family tells you, before you look at a single chart, roughly how expensive and how jumpy a pair will be.

children.text: Where the World's Money Actually Trades

body.title: Share of Global FX Turnover by Currency Pair, April 2025 (%)

children.text: Every one of the world's ten most traded pairs includes the US dollar, according to the BIS. EUR/USD alone accounts for about a fifth of all forex trading. Notice USD/CNY in third place, ahead of GBP/USD. China's renminbi is technically an emerging-market currency with capital controls, yet it now outtrades the British pound as a pair. Size of the economy and trade links can push a currency up the table.

body.title: Size of the biggest pair
body.prompt: Global forex turnover was $9.6 trillion a day in April 2025, and EUR/USD made up 21.2% of it. How many billion dollars of EUR/USD traded per day? Round to the nearest billion.
body.explanation: $9,600 billion × 21.2% = $2,035.2 billion, a little over $2 trillion a day in one currency pair. For scale, that is roughly 160 times NSE's average daily cash market turnover of about $12.6 billion from Chapter 1.

stats.label: US dollar
stats.context: Share of global FX turnover, April 2025

body.title: Why currency shares add up to 200%, not 100%

children.text: Every forex trade involves two currencies. A single $1 million EUR/USD trade counts once for the euro and once for the dollar. So when the BIS measures what share of trades each currency appears in, the shares of all currencies add up to 200%. The dollar's 89.2% means it is on one side of 89.2% of all trades. Pair shares, like EUR/USD at 21.2%, count each trade once, so those add up to 100%.
Majors: Cheap to Trade, Hard to Outsmart

The majors are the currencies of large, open economies with free capital movement and deep bond markets. They trade around the clock, spreads are tiny, and prices rarely jump without news. The flip side is that thousands of banks, hedge funds and algorithms analyse them every second, so easy edges are rare. Dealers even have nicknames for them, which you will hear in market commentary.

children.text: Crosses: Built From Two Dollar Pairs

You learned cross rates in the first lesson of this chapter. EUR/JPY is simply EUR/USD multiplied by USD/JPY. What that lesson did not show is the cost. If a cross is priced through two dollar pairs, it inherits both of their spreads. You buy the euro at the EUR/USD ask and buy yen-priced euros at the USD/JPY ask, so the gaps stack up.

body.latex: \text{EUR/JPY ask} = \text{EUR/USD ask} \times \text{USD/JPY ask} \qquad \text{EUR/JPY bid} = \text{EUR/USD bid} \times \text{USD/JPY bid}
body.caption: A synthetic cross takes the worse side of both legs

body.title: Price the cross
body.prompt: EUR/USD is quoted at 1.1599 / 1.1601 and USD/JPY at 149.99 / 150.01. Each has a 2-pip spread. What is the EUR/JPY ask if built through the dollar? Round to two decimals.
body.explanation: EUR/JPY ask = 1.1601 × 150.01 = 174.03 (174.0266 unrounded). The bid is 1.1599 × 149.99 = 173.97 (173.9734 unrounded). The EUR/JPY spread is about 0.053, or roughly 5 yen pips, more than double the 2-pip spread on each leg. In practice, busy crosses like EUR/JPY also trade directly, which keeps real spreads tighter, but the principle holds: crosses cost more than majors.

body.title: Name the family
body.question: A trader on a global platform is watching GBP/JPY. Which family does this pair belong to?
options: Major, because both are big currencies
Cross, because it pairs two majors without the US dollar
Exotic, because the yen is Asian
Rupee pair, because it is available in India
body.explanation: GBP/JPY combines two major currencies and leaves out the dollar, which makes it a cross. Being Asian does not make the yen exotic. It is the third most traded currency in the world.

children.text: Exotics: Where Prices Can Break

Emerging-market currencies trade less, so spreads are wider. Many come with capital controls, central bank intervention and offshore NDF markets, all of which you have already seen with the rupee. The biggest risk is sudden repricing. The Turkish lira lost about 44% of its value against the dollar in 2021 as inflation soared and interest rates were cut. Over the same year, the rupee weakened by less than 2%. Both are emerging-market currencies, but they are not remotely the same risk.

children.text: So Where Does the Rupee Fit?

markDefs.definition: An exchange rate regime where the market sets the price, but the central bank intervenes to smooth excessive volatility. India follows this approach.

children.text: By textbook definition, USD/INR is an emerging-market pair. The rupee is fully convertible for trade but not fully for capital flows, it runs a
managed float

, and it has an active offshore NDF market. But it is a heavyweight within that group. It sits around 11th among all currencies, with about $185 billion of rupee trading a day onshore and offshore, and RBI's reserves and intervention have historically kept its moves far calmer than those of many peers. Think of it as a large, managed emerging-market currency rather than a wild exotic.

body.label: The rupee's place in global forex
body.context: BIS Triennial Survey, April 2025. That is roughly $185 billion a day including offshore trading, up from $119 billion in 2022, and behind the dollar, euro, yen, pound, renminbi and several smaller developed-market currencies.

body.title: Milestones in the Rupee's Global Role

events.title: Current account convertibility
events.description: India accepts IMF Article VIII obligations, making the rupee freely convertible for trade and other current transactions.

events.title: USD/INR futures on NSE
events.description: An exchange-traded, regulated rupee contract becomes available to Indian investors.

events.title: Cross-currency derivatives in India
events.description: NSE launches futures and options on EUR/USD, GBP/USD and USD/JPY, letting residents trade major pairs on a regulated exchange.

events.title: Trade settlement in rupees
events.description: RBI sets up a framework for invoicing and settling international trade in rupees.

events.title: India and UAE local currency settlement
events.description: The two countries agree a framework to settle trade directly in rupees and dirhams.

events.title: Bond index inclusion
events.description: Indian government bonds enter JP Morgan's emerging-market bond index, drawing foreign investors to rupee assets.

events.title: Rupee at 1.9% of global turnover

body.text: Watch the jargon. Globally, a "cross" means a pair without the US dollar, like EUR/GBP. On Indian exchanges, "cross currency" means a pair without the rupee, so EUR/USD, a global major, is listed as a cross currency contract on NSE. Same word, different meaning depending on who is speaking.

If an app lets an Indian resident trade AUD/USD, GBP/JPY, USD/TRY or gold with high leverage outside NSE or BSE, it is not a legal route under FEMA, no matter how professional it looks. Exotic pairs on those platforms add a second problem: very wide spreads and weekend gaps that can wipe out an account before you can react.

body.title: The guru's watchlist
body.scenario: Nikhil, a 26-year-old engineer in Hyderabad, follows an Instagram trader who posts daily calls on GBP/JPY and USD/TRY through an offshore app with 1:1000 leverage. The trader says USD/TRY is "the best pair for beginners because it only goes up." The app shows a USD/TRY spread of 150 pips, while EUR/USD shows 0.8 pips. Nikhil also has a Zerodha account with currency derivatives activated.
body.prompt: Classify both pairs, explain the risks in the guru's advice, and suggest what Nikhil could do instead if he wants to learn to trade a major pair legally.
body.modelAnswer:
1. GBP/JPY is a cross: two majors, no US dollar. USD/TRY is an exotic: the dollar against an emerging-market currency with a history of sharp devaluations.
2. "Only goes up" describes a currency that has been losing value, not a safe trade. Exotics can also reverse suddenly after policy changes or intervention, and 1:1000 leverage means a 0.1% move against Nikhil wipes out his margin.
3. A 150-pip spread means he starts every USD/TRY trade deep in loss. That is nearly 190 times the 0.8-pip EUR/USD spread on the same app.
4. Trading forex through an offshore leveraged app is not a legal route for Indian residents under FEMA, regardless of the pair.
5. Instead, he can learn on NSE's cross currency contracts on EUR/USD, GBP/USD or USD/JPY through his Zerodha account, with exchange-set margins, a regulated clearing corporation and small lot sizes, after finishing the chapters on leverage and risk. Rupee pairs such as USD/INR are not an option for him, because they may be used only to hedge a genuine currency exposure.

body.title: Name the group
body.textWithBlank: Pairs made of the US dollar and a heavily traded developed-market currency, such as EUR/USD and USD/JPY, are called ___.
body.explanation: Majors are the most liquid, lowest-spread pairs in the world. All of them include the US dollar.

cards.definition: The US dollar with EUR, JPY, GBP, CHF, CAD, AUD or NZD. Deepest liquidity and tightest spreads.
A pair of two majors without the US dollar, such as EUR/GBP or GBP/JPY.
A contract on a pair without the rupee: EUR/USD, GBP/USD or USD/JPY.
A major currency against a smaller or emerging-market currency. Wider spreads and higher gap risk.
Market nickname for GBP/USD, from the transatlantic telegraph cable once used to transmit its price.
A market-set exchange rate with central bank intervention to curb excessive volatility, as with the rupee.

points: Currency pairs fall into three families: majors (USD with a major developed currency), crosses (two majors without USD) and exotics (a major with a smaller or emerging currency).
All ten of the world's most traded pairs include the US dollar, and EUR/USD alone is about 21% of global turnover.
Crosses priced through the dollar inherit the spreads of both legs, so they cost more to trade than majors.
Exotics carry wider spreads, policy risk and sudden gaps. The Turkish lira lost about 44% against the dollar in 2021.
The rupee is a large, managed emerging-market currency with a 1.9% share of global turnover, about 11th in the world.
On NSE, "cross currency" means a pair without the rupee, such as EUR/USD, which is different from the global meaning of cross.

Residents can trade EUR/USD, GBP/USD and USD/JPY on Indian exchanges within exchange limits, and can use rupee-pair contracts only to hedge a genuine currency exposure. Other pairs on offshore leveraged apps are not a legal route.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment or trading advice. Turnover shares are from the BIS Triennial Survey of April 2025 and secondary summaries of it. Spreads and quotes are illustrative. Contract lists and specifications can change, so confirm current details on the NSE and BSE websites before trading.
